items.title: MSF MOZAMBIQUE: Teams bring healthcare closer to communities as barriers to care persist
items.blurb:
Country: Mozambique
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

With just one functioning health centre serving more than 138,000 people in Macomia district, Médecins Sans Frontières / Doctors Without Borders (MSF) brings primary and specialised care closer to communities, including people living with HIV. Yet these efforts cannot replace a functioning, well-resourced health system.

For people in Macomia, seeking healthcare often means making a long, costly and sometimes dangerous journey to the district’s only functioning health facility. Upon reaching it, they may find that the medicines, tests or specialised care they need are not available.

First person testimonies available here: http://prez.ly/Odqe

Macomia district covers about 4,000 km² and is home to an estimated 138,565 people1. Before the armed conflict in Cabo Delgado started in 2017, there were seven health facilities across the district; todayonly one remains functioning. It must serve residents, returnees and thousands of families displaced by insecurity2. In this region, conflict involving Islamic State Mozambique (ISM), national and regional forces affects people’s daily lives through attacks and fear of renewed violence, kidnappings and roadblocks.

Since 2019, MSF has helped to sustain access to healthcare in Macomia, adapting our services after a major attack by ISM on the town in 2024 forced a temporary suspension of activities. Having previously run our own clinic in Macomia town, MSF shifted to providing technical support to the Ministry of Health’s health centre with emergency care, maternal and child health services, while facilitating referrals to Pemba and running mobile clinics. Serving over 30,000 people, mobile clinics provide preventive and curative primary healthcare, including consultations, paediatric and basic emergency care, maternal health support, malaria diagnosis and treatment, HIV/TB screening and referral, nutrition support, mental health care, psychosocial support and health promotion. From January to September 2026, MSF teams carried out over 24,000 outpatient consultations in mobile clinics – the equivalent of around 90 consultations per day. ​

Respiratory infections were the most common condition treated, followed by malaria, which remains a major health burden in Mozambique. Over the same period, MSF teams carried out almost 9,000 sexual and reproductive health consultations and assisted 3,130 births. We also provided more than 700 mental health consultations, reinforcing a critical service in a context where needs are high but often go undetected and unmet. With only one psychiatrist based in Pemba serving a province of 2.8 million people, specialised care and referral options remain limited.

Many factors keep health care out of reach

In Macomia, multiple barriers keep people cut off from even the most basic healthcare. ​

The first barrier is reaching care at all. Distances, insecurity on the roads and damaged or non-functioning infrastructure make access difficult or impossible for many. With few and unreliable public transport options, people have to look for private means when they are already sick or in need of urgent care. ​

In many cases, the decisive obstacle iscost. A round trip from Nacate, a populated area 16.5 km away, to Macomia health centre can cost up to 1,000 meticais (about 15 USD), an unaffordable amount in a country where 81 per cent of the population lives on less than three dollars a day3.

“For a woman in labour, for a couple, for a family with a daughter who needs care, finding that amount is not easy,” says Laura Eugénio, an MSF staff member working in sexual and reproductive health in Macomia.

Recent increases in fuel price, amounting to around 12 per cent for petrol and 45 per cent for diesel4, have made this financial pressure even worse.

Reaching the health centre does not guarantee access to care. Shortages of medicines, tests and medical supplies add another barrier to diagnosis and treatment. This is a country-wide challenge and the effects are even more acute in remote and insecure districts such as Macomia. Between July and October, essential medicines that ran out included painkillers and fever reducers, antibiotics, iron and folic acid supplements – used to treat fever and infections, support maternal health and provide preventive care. ​

Shortages of rapid tests, medical and surgical supplies limited the care that health workers could provide during routine consultations. Specialised services can also be compromised. Against a backdrop of reported shortages of HIV testing kits in 93 of Cabo Delgado’s 103 health facilities, screening coverage among pregnant women with unknown HIV status at Macomia health centre’s maternity department remained below the 95 per cent target. Consistent testing is essential to offer timely treatment that protects women’s health and helps prevent mother-to-child transmission.

Staying on HIV treatment amid violence, fear and stigma

Beyond testing, insecurity and stigma disrupt HIV prevention and treatment. Attacks by ISM and fear of renewed violence can force people to flee at short notice, making it harder to stay on medication.

“I keep my medicines and my documents somewhere easy to reach,” says Suleimani, a person living with HIV in the district. “If there is an attack while I am at home, I run to take everything with me into the bush, because I now understand how important it is not to miss my medication. But not everyone is aware of that.” ​

Stigma around HIV remains widespread, and the act of seeking care itself may expose patients to discrimination. With services concentrated in the district’s only functioning health centre, confidentiality has become harder to guarantee. Some patients worry they will be recognised when attending follow-up appointments or collecting medication. ​

“Many people stop going to pick up their medicines at Macomia health centre because they fear discrimination” explains Suleimani. “There is a door at the hospital and people know that whoever goes through it is going for HIV treatment. That exposes people.” ​

Maintaining continuity of care remains a major challenge: among patients who started HIV treatment between July 2025 and March 2026, only just over half were still receiving care six months later. To help bring patients back into care, MSF health promotion teams actively trace HIV patients considered “lost to follow up” – meaning they have not shown up to their appointments for more than 61 days. Since August, more than half of the people traced have decided to return to treatment, with MSF staff accompanying them through the first steps of the process. ​

Expanding options for care

Referral data point to a high and sustained demand for obstetric care: of the 187 referrals recorded from January to September 2026, 120 were for complicated deliveries. Nearly half of the pregnant women referred to Pemba were under 20. With only one ambulance in Macomia, each transfer to Pemba leaves no other vehicle available. In September 2026, MSF completed the construction of an operating theatre attached to Macomia health centre, designed to manage complicated pregnancies and other surgical emergencies locally, reducing risky and costly transfers and improving access to timely care for mothers and newborns. ​

Given the many barriers to accessing healthcare services, MSF mobile clinics are often the only way to receive care for people in more remote parts of the district.

“There are few options left. People stay home until they get better or until it’s too late”,says Samuel, a 64-year-old patient from Nacate.

They are also instrumental in identifying patients who need higher-level care and organising referrals and transport. ​

Mobile clinics cannot replace a well-resourced health system

In recent weeks, MSF teams have observed increased attendance at some of the mobile clinics that we run outside Macomia town, putting extra strain on services designed for more remote communities. As vital as they are, mobile clinics should not be a substitute for a functioning health system. They can help reduce some of the barriers people face, but they cannot replace a network of health facilities, reliable supply chains, infrastructure and trained staff. ​

In Cabo Delgado, where conflict remains the main driver of displacement, insecurity continues to affect every aspect of people’s lives, including seeking care. Authorities have a responsibility to protect health facilities, strengthen supply chains and ensure safe access for patients and health workers. ​

Availability of water is also a critical unmet need in many communities. Without water and adequate sanitation and hygiene services, the risk of waterborne diseases increases, placing further pressure on the few functioning health facilities. Improving these conditions in communities and facilities is essential to deliver care. ​

Donors must support sustained healthcare and humanitarian presence in districts such as Macomia, which risk becoming even more isolated as funding shrinks. Without this combination of commitment from authorities and humanitarian support, people already affected by nearly a decade of conflict will continue to remain cut off and face preventable suffering.

In Cabo Delgado province, MSF also works in Mocímboa da Praia, providing technical support to the hospital and to the three functioning health centres in the district, out of a total of eight.

items.title: World: Qatar Charity’s Information and Crisis Management Center Supports Faster Humanitarian Response [EN/AR]

As natural disasters and conflicts drive displacement and increase relief needs, Qatar Charity has established an Information and Crisis Management Center to support its humanitarian operations. Launched in June 2026, the Center is one of the organization’s major humanitarian digital transformation initiatives.

According to a report published on the Ghiras website, the Centre brings together data, advanced technology, and artificial intelligence to improve response times, strengthen planning, and make humanitarian interventions more effective in crisis- and disaster-affected areas.

According to a report on the Ghiras website, the Center reflects the organization’s commitment to using data, technology, and artificial intelligence to support humanitarian action, improve planning, and enable more timely and effective interventions in crisis- and disaster-affected regions.

Why Was the Center Established?

The Center was established in response to several rapidly evolving global challenges:

  • Increasing climate-related disasters.
  • Escalating conflicts and the displacement they cause.
  • The need for real-time information to inform decisions.
  • The importance of rapid intervention during the first hours of a crisis.
  • The growing role of technology and artificial intelligence in humanitarian action.
  • The need for stronger coordination among headquarters, field offices, and partners.

What Does the Center Aim to Achieve?

The Center pursues several strategic objectives:

  • Strengthening Qatar Charity’s preparedness for emergencies and disasters.
  • Developing an early-warning system for humanitarian crises.
  • Providing senior management and field teams with accurate data and analysis.
  • Improving the efficiency of humanitarian interventions and supporting faster responses.
  • Improving resource management and identifying humanitarian priorities.
  • Strengthening coordination among relevant stakeholders.
  • Building an institutional record of crises and lessons learned.

How Does the Center Work?

The Center uses an integrated system for monitoring, analysis, and information management. Its work includes monitoring crises and disasters around the clock, collecting and analyzing data from multiple sources, and preparing regular reports and urgent updates.

From late August through September 2026, it monitored severe flooding across large parts of Nepal, gathering and analyzing information on the evolving situation and the needs of affected communities. In September 2026, the Center also monitored the arrival of a new wave of Yemeni refugees in Djibouti following renewed conflict. Its ongoing monitoring and analysis of humanitarian conditions and urgent needs supported relief efforts, coordination, and operational decision-making.

What Sets the Center Apart?

Supporting the 2026–2030 Strategy

items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

Please refer to the attached file.

In Ukraine Civilians Die at Alarming Rates Amid Intensifying Attacks, UN Human Rights Officials Say

Kyiv, November 17, 2026 -- Powerful weapons of war kill ever growing numbers of civilians across Ukraine, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) said today. Attacks in October alone left at least 372 civilians dead and 1,981 injured HRMMU reported in its monthly update.

The report notes that the number of killed and injured in October of this year was 95 per cent higher than in October 2025. The latest figures show that this year has seen significantly higher casualties than previous years.

The alarming trend continued in November which saw one of the deadliest single attacks for civilians since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. On 2 November multiple bombs struck the premises of a school, including an underground shelter in Komyshuvakha in south-eastern Ukraine, where civilians had gathered to receive humanitarian assistance. Ukrainian authorities announced on 16 November that 72 people had died in the attack and that four others were still missing. HRMMU continues to verify the identity and status of those killed, but has already confirmed that dozens of them were civilians, including local residents, local administration staff and emergency workers.

"The first ten months of this year have seen more civilian deaths than all of 2025, which in turn was worse than the year before," said Danielle Bell who heads HRMMU. "The world should not become numb to the deadly toll the war exacts on Ukraine's civilians," she said.

Long-range weapons (missiles and drones) remain the leading cause of civilian casualties, accounting for more than half of those killed and injured.

In October, casualties from aerial glide bombs increased, with the number of civilians killed doubling compared with September, reaching 92 killed and 331 injured. Aerial glide bombs and short-range drones accounted for nearly equal shares of civilian casualties, 18 and 19 per cent, respectively. In October, Russian armed forces significantly intensified attacks on energy infrastructure across Ukraine as the country braces for its fifth winter at war. The attacks damaged electricity and heating infrastructure, temporarily disrupting power and, in some cities, also water supply, forcing Ukrainian authorities to introduce rolling power outages across the country. Ukrainian armed forces also attacked electricity infrastructure in Russian-occupied territory of Ukraine.

Meanwhile according to public statements by Russian authorities on individual incidents in October, at least 90 people were killed and 306 injured in occupied territory and at least 59 people were killed and 402 injured in the Russian Federation as a result of Ukrainian attacks, but HRMMU is not able to verify the figures because of lack of access and independent sources of information. In territory of Ukraine occupied by Russia HRMMU verified that at least 12 civilians were killed and 18 injured.

In all 17,994 civilians have been killed and 57,854 have been injured in Ukraine since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022.

Note: HRMMU will publish its findings related to the attack in Komyshuvakha in due course.

items.title: WHO calls for urgent, sustained support to protect essential health services in Sudan
items.blurb:
Country: Sudan
Source: World Health Organization

17 November 2026, Khartoum, Sudan – The World Health Organization (WHO) is calling for sustained support to keep essential health services functioning in Sudan’s White Nile and North Kordofan states, where conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and shortages of medicines and power continue to strain the health system.

The call follows a WHO mission to Kosti in White Nile State, and to El Obeid, North Kordofan’s capital, from 7 to 12 November, led by WHO Representative in Sudan Dr Abdinasir Abubakar.

“The health needs I witnessed in White Nile and North Kordofan are immense. We urgently need to scale up essential health services in peripheral localities and displacement camps,” said Dr Abdinasir. “Despite enormous challenges, health workers and partners remain committed to serving the most vulnerable communities. We must match their commitment with sustained support.”

Prolonged conflict, displacement, food insecurity, disease outbreaks and malnutrition have severely disrupted health services. Across Sudan, 21 million people need health assistance, while 37% of health facilities are non-functional.

The mission highlighted continuing gaps in electricity supplies, medicines, operational resources and access to care in both states. Power interruptions continue to disrupt critical services, including operating theatres, intensive care, neonatal incubators, oxygen generation, blood banks, dialysis and laboratory services, putting patients at risk. Reliable power, including solarization, is urgently needed to sustain lifesaving services.

White Nile State hosts more than 216 000 internally displaced people and nearly 455 000 refugees – approximately half of Sudan’s refugee population – placing considerable pressure on already strained health services.

In North Kordofan, prolonged conflict, displacement, food insecurity and economic hardship are exacerbating health and nutrition needs. El Obeid hosts most of the over 141 000 internally displaced people in Sheikan locality, further straining already overstretched health services.

WHO support to Kosti Teaching Hospital reached more than 24 000 people between November 2025 and April 2026. WHO also supported oxygen-cylinder refills, provided three oxygen concentrators and installed solar capacity in the Emergency Department. A separate solar system at Kosti Renal Dialysis Centre is helping sustain lifesaving emergency dialysis services during frequent power outages.

In El Obeid, WHO support in 2025–2026 has contributed to approximately 344 500 health services, including 90 000 patient consultations. WHO also provided over 9000 litres of fuel to help maintain electricity at El Obeid Teaching Hospital, alongside medicines, supplies, capacity-building and operational support.

During the mission, Dr Abdinasir met with state government officials, health authorities, WHO teams and humanitarian partners to review priority needs and ongoing humanitarian response and recovery interventions. In Kosti, he opened a training workshop on Ebola virus disease preparedness, and in El Obeid he joined the monthly Health Cluster meeting with six health partners to strengthen coordination and the collective health response.

WHO calls for urgent, sustained flexible funding to maintain and expand essential health services, support frontline health workers, strengthen outbreak preparedness and response and ensure reliable medical supplies, power and emergency referral systems. Safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access and the protection of health workers, patients and health facilities are also crucial.

WHO continues to work with health authorities, communities, Health Cluster partners and donors to sustain lifesaving services and support the recovery of Sudan’s health system.

items.blurb:
Country: Côte d'Ivoire
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

FOOD SECURITY SNAPSHOT

  • Cereal production forecast above average in 2026
  • Prices of rice near or below year-earlier levels
  • About 1.3 million people severely acute food insecure during 2026 lean season

Cereal production forecast above average in 2026

In southern bimodal rainfall areas, harvesting of the 2026 main season maize and rice crops was completed in September. Generally favorable weather conditions between March and July 2026 supported crop establishment and development. However, heavy rains in June and July triggered localized flooding, particularly around Abidjan, damaging crops in some areas. Planting of the secondary-season maize and rice crops was also completed in September. Below-average cumulative precipitation amounts between September and October constrained planting operations and early crop development in several areas. Weather forecasts indicate a high likelihood of above-average rainfall amounts in November across most producing regions, which are expected to improve crop conditions, while increasing the risk of localized flooding. By contrast, below-average precipitation amounts are forecast in some minor producing coastal areas.

In northern unimodal rainfall areas, harvesting of the 2026 coarse grain and rice crops is underway and expected to conclude by year-end. The May-October rainy season started on time or up to three weeks earlier than usual in some areas, supporting planting operations and crop establishment. Near-average cumulative rainfall amounts through October were generally conducive to crop development, and production prospects are favorable.

Aggregate cereal production in 2026 is preliminarily forecast at about 4.4 million tonnes, approximately 20 percent above the average of the previous five years. The good output mainly reflects an expansion in planted area, officially estimated at 25 percent above average, supported by government programmes providing agricultural inputs and machinery to farmers in collaboration with technical and financial partners.

Prices of rice near or below year-earlier levels

Prices of locally produced rice, a key staple food, were generally stable between June and September 2026, with seasonal increases of up to 5 percent recorded in some markets. Despite these increases, prices in September were near or up to 10 percent below their year-earlier levels across monitored markets.

About 1.3 million people severely acute food insecure during 2026 lean season

According to the latest Cadre Harmonisé (CH) analysis, about 1.3 million people (5 percent of the analysed population) were estimated to face severe acute food insecurity (CH Phase 3 [Crisis] and above) during the June-August 2026 lean season, including more than 14 500 people in CH Phase 4 (Emergency). This represents a slight improvement from the same period in 2025, when approximately 1.4 million people (6 percent of the analysed population) were estimated to face CH Phase 3 (Crisis) and above.

Spillover effects of the conflict in the Central Sahel remain a major driver of acute food insecurity in northern areas, particularly in the Tchologo and Bounkani regions, where 12 and 14 percent of the analysed population, respectively, were estimated to be in CH Phase 3 (Crisis) and above. These regions host about 85 percent of the country’s 88 000 registered refugees and asylum seekers, while continued arrivals from Burkina Faso and Mali are placing additional pressure on natural resources and livelihoods in host communities. Persistent insecurity in border areas is also restricting access to farmland and pastures and disrupting food supplies to local markets, where elevated prices have been reported.

Households’ economic access to food also remains a concern. The guaranteed farmgate price of cocoa, the country’s main export crop, for the 2026/27 main marketing season is 57 percent below the level set at the start of the previous marketing season and is expected to reduce incomes among households dependent on cocoa production. In addition, recent increases in domestic diesel prices, linked to high international oil prices, have raised transport costs and may exert upward pressure on food prices, further constraining households’ purchasing power.

Flooding in southern areas affected about 21 500 people in 2026 and caused damage to homes, productive assets, crops and road infrastructure. The resulting disruptions to trade flows and market supplies contributed to localized food price increases.

Vue d’ensemble

L’analyse de la situation nutritionnelle révèle une situation précaire sur l’ensemble du territoire avec une prédominance des zones en situation d’Alerte nutritionnelle. Pour la période de juin à novembre 2026, les communes d’Arcahaie, Cabaret et Cité Soleil se trouvent en situation nutritionnelle Sérieuse (Phase 3 de l’IPC), principalement à cause de la situation sécuritaire, de l’insécurité alimentaire persistante et du poids des phénomènes morbides. Par ailleurs, 59 communes sont placées en état d’Alerte nutritionnelle (Phase 2 de l’IPC), tandis que cinq départements et sept communes affichent une situation Acceptable (Phase 1 de l’IPC).

Pour la période projetée de décembre 2026 à mai 2027, une nette dégradation de la situation nutritionnelle est attendue en lien avec une dégradation probable des conditions sécuritaires, socio-politiques, épidémiologiques et climatiques. Les communes de Cabaret et Cité Soleil basculeront en situation Critique (Phase 4 de l’IPC), tandis qu’Arcahaie est susceptible de se maintenir en situation Sérieuse (Phase 3 de l’IPC), rejointe par 28 autres communes qui quitteront la phase d’Alerte pour la phase Sérieuse. Parallèlement, les départements des Nippes, du Nord-Est et du Sud-Est, ainsi que cinq communes, passeront de la situation Acceptable à la situation d’Alerte, où se maintiennent déjà 31 autres communes. En revanche, la situation restera Acceptable (Phase 1 de l’IPC) pour les départements du Nord et du Sud, ainsi que pour deux communes du département de l’Ouest.

Par ailleurs, sur la période de juin 2026 à mai 2027, plus de 253 700cas de malnutrition aiguë globale (modérée et sévère) sont attendus chez les enfants de 6 à 59 mois. Parmi eux, près de 93 900 enfants risquent de souffrir de malnutrition aiguë sévère, une forme particulièrement critique qui augmente fortement le risque de mortalité.

Il est enfin important de noter que l’analyse n’a pas permis d’examiner de manière désagrégée certains groupes particulièrement vulnérables, notamment les personnes déplacées internes (PDI). Une mise à jour plus granulaire apparaît donc nécessaire afin de mieux appréhender leurs vulnérabilités spécifiques et d’orienter plus efficacement les interventions en fonction de leurs besoins. La réalisation rapide d’une enquête nutritionnelle est indispensable pour mesurer l’ampleur de la crise et optimiser le déploiement des interventions d’aide.

Partout dans le pays, l’impact direct de la crise sécuritaire avec les déplacements de population et l’insécurité alimentaire persistante, exacerbée par les chocs climatiques et la crise économique, dégrade fortement la situation nutritionnelle. À cela s’ajoutent des déterminants majeurs tels que la forte morbidité infantile (paludisme, diarrhées, infections respiratoires) et les épidémies récurrentes de choléra, ainsi que les carences liées à l’alimentation et aux pratiques de soin (faiblesse de l’allaitement maternel exclusif).

La deuxième édition de l’analyse IPC de la malnutrition aiguë (IPC MNA) en Haïti a couvert l’ensemble des 10 départements du pays. L’analyse a été menée à l’échelle départementale pour les Nippes, le Nord, le Nord-Est, le Sud et le Sud-Est, tandis qu’elle s’est faite à l’échelle communale (couvrant 69 communes) pour l’Artibonite, le Centre, la Grand’Anse, l’Ouest et le Nord-Ouest.

Les facteurs contributifs à cette situation nutritionnelle précaire varient selon les zones analysées. Dans les zones classées en Phase 3 de l’IPC, les principaux facteurs contributifs sont l’insécurité résiduelle, la précarité de la consommation alimentaire des enfants et l’insécurité alimentaire persistante. S’y ajoutent une forte prévalence des infections respiratoires aiguës et de la fièvre, la faiblesse de la couverture sanitaire ainsi que de mauvaises conditions d’hygiène.

items.blurb:
Countries: South Sudan, Ethiopia
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

23-12-2025

What happened, where and when?

The Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak was declared in Ethiopia on 14 November 2025, prompting heightened preparedness measures in neighboring South Sudan due to the risk of cross-border transmission through frequent population movement, trade, and pastoral migration. On 23 December 2025, three suspected MVD-related deaths were reported in Kapoeta East County, including two individuals with a recent travel history to the affected areas of Ethiopia and one suspected community-linked case. These alerts triggered increased preparedness and readiness efforts by the South Sudan Red Cross (SSRC) in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and partners.

The operation was implemented from 30 December 2025 to 28 February 2026 in the high-risk border counties of Akobo, Maiwut, Pibor, and Kapoeta East, which had been identified as priority locations because of their proximity to Ethiopia and high levels of cross-border movement. Preparedness activities included volunteer training, community-based surveillance, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), infection prevention and control (IPC), hygiene promotion, and Safe and Dignified Burial (SDB) preparedness.

During implementation, the epidemiological situation remained stable and no confirmed MVD cases were reported in South Sudan. Investigations into suspected alerts, including those reported in Kapoeta East, did not result in any confirmed Marburg cases, and one suspected alert investigated during the operation tested negative. However, operational challenges affected implementation. In Akobo and Maiwut, insecurity and localized conflict restricted access to some communities and required volunteers and staff to relocate temporarily to safer locations while continuing awareness activities where feasible. In Pibor, cattle-raiding incidents disrupted planned interventions and limited access to some target areas. In Kapoeta East, poor road conditions and the remoteness of border communities presented logistical challenges, although SSRC successfully reached border locations, trained volunteers, and implemented preparedness activities.

By the end of the operation, no confirmed MVD cases had been detected in South Sudan. The outbreak situation in Ethiopia had improved, transmission had been brought under control, and preparedness capacities in the targeted counties had been strengthened through trained volunteers, community awareness, surveillance systems, IPC measures, and SDB readiness mechanisms.

items.title: Afghanistan: Children on the Move: Displacement Leaves Afghan Children Hungrier and More Vulnerable, Save the Children Warns
items.blurb:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: Save the Children

KABUL, 18 November 2026 – More than half of children displaced in Afghanistan said they have less food to eat since leaving their homes, while two in five reported worsening health, according to a new Save the Children report that reveals the severe toll displacement is taking on children across the country.

The “Children on the Move” report, based on interviews with more than 800 children and caregivers in seven provinces in Afghanistan, found that displacement over the past three years has deepened hunger, disrupted education and exposed children to heightened protection risks. More than nine in 10 children surveyed had experienced displacement or migration.

More than half (55%) of children said they had less food to eat after moving, 41% said their health had deteriorated, and a third (33%) of caregivers said children's access to education had worsened.

But despite growing needs, support is failing to reach many children. Fewer than one in 10 children surveyed said they had received any assistance, while nine in 10 said they needed support to access food.

The findings come after more than 6.67 million Afghans have returned from Pakistan and Iran since September 2023 – increasing the population by up to 14% - and putting greater pressure on families and communities already struggling with poverty, food insecurity and repeated crises. [2].

Afghanistan also has one of the highest rates of internal displacement globally, with about 7 million people, or around 14% of the population, displaced as of 2025. [3].

Economic hardship is the main driver of displacement in Afghanistan. Nearly half of children (49%) said their families moved because they could not find work or earn enough income, while a third cited food shortages. Almost one in four said their families had relocated due to deportation or pressure to leave another country.

Nearly seven out of 10 children surveyed have endured two or more crises in the last three years, including drought, floods, earthquakes and conflict.

Compounding crises and displacement are affecting children’s wellbeing in Afghanistan, with children facing growing protection risks. Just over one in 10 (11%) said they had been exposed to at least one protection risk, including child labour, physical or verbal violence or early marriage. Caregivers reported that girls faced particularly high risks during displacement journeys and after arriving in new locations.

Among those affected is Nooria*, 8, who arrived in Afghanistan for this first time earlier this year after her family left Pakistan where they had built their lives over five decades. Nooria*, her parents and three siblings arrived with little more than the clothes they carried.

Nooria* said:

“We returned from Pakistan. We had a home there, and I had many friends. I like Afghanistan too, but I miss my school and my friends. We used to play together and laugh a lot.

“We want to have a school like the one we had in Pakistan, where we can continue our education.”

Nooria’s family cannot afford the transport costs to send her to school, but she attends classes at a Save the Children temporary learning space. Her mother, Nazoo*, 28, said:

“My husband does not have a job here, and we have no source of income to provide for our children's needs. I worry every day about how we will find food for our next meal.

“When you are born in a country and get married there, that place becomes your home. You feel that you belong there. When you suddenly have to leave, your whole life falls apart, especially when you arrive with nothing.”

The ‘Children on the Move’ report found that assistance reaching children is extremely limited, with significant gaps between needs and the support they receive.

Ashish Damle, Country Director, Save the Children in Afghanistan said:

“No child should have to abandon their homes, schools and communities for safety or survival - but for many, displacement has become part of their childhood. Children face dangerous journeys with serious protection risks, only to arrive in places where their families are still struggling to put food on the table, access healthcare and send them to school.

“Our ‘Children on the Move’ research reveals a deeply concerning reality - finding a new home does not mean reaching safety. Girls and children with disabilities in particular face greater protection risks, while poverty is forcing families to make impossible choices just to survive, often with little or no humanitarian assistance.

“Children who have already lost their homes should not be left to face these risks alone. We urgently need sustained funding to protect them along migration routes and ensure they can access essential services wherever they settle.

“These children deserve more than day to day survival. They deserve the chance to feel safe, return to school and rebuild their lives.”

Save the Children has been working in Afghanistan since 1976, including through periods of conflict, displacement and natural disasters. We currently run programmes in nine provinces and work with partners across an additional 11 provinces, delivering services in health, nutrition, education, child protection, shelter, water, sanitation, hygiene and livelihoods.

items.title: EU advances Syrian recovery and reconstruction through Syria Partnership Coordination Forum in Damascus
items.blurb:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: European Commission

Please refer to the attached file.

Today, the Syria Partnership Coordination Forum (SPCF) convened in Damascus for the first time to advance Syria's recovery and reconstruction, showcase investment opportunities and agree on concrete steps forward.

The SPCF brought together key partners, including EU Member States, the G7, Arab countries, and the UN and International Financial Institutions, such as the World Bank, the European Investment Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the Islamic Development Bank, as well as civil society, to discuss Syria's business environment and steps to translate Syria's priorities into concrete investment opportunities.

The Forum, co-chaired by Syria and the EU, was opened by Commissioner for the Mediterranean Dubravka Šuica and the Syrian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Assaad Al-Shaibani.

Economic revitalisation, institutional recovery and improved livelihoods

In her second visit to the country, Commissioner Šuica officially launched the Syria Technical Assistance Hub to support Syrian institutions in strengthening their capacities and advancing reforms that are instrumental to restore confidence, attract responsible investment and support sustainable economic recovery.

The Commissioner also witnessed the signing of new EU-funded contracts supporting Syria's recovery and reconstruction, namely on the rule of law, on an enabling business environment andon support to small and medium-sized enterprises. These initiatives will help revive the economy, strengthen public institutions and improve livelihoods. By helping businesses access finance and grow, the projects can create jobs and improve conditions for investment. They will also improve access to justice, supporting a recovery that benefits people across Syria.

During her bilateral meeting with Minister Al-Shaibani, Commissioner Šuica received Syria's signed undertaking to implement the EU's Registered Exporter system. This marks an important step towards enabling Syrian products to benefit from preferential access to the EU market under the Generalised Scheme of Preferences, opening up new opportunities for Syrian exporters and supporting the country's economic recovery.

Commissioner Šuica also visited the Deir Ali Power Plant together with Ibrahim Al-Adhan, Syrian Deputy Minister of Energy and EIB Vice President Gelsomina Vigliotti. The visit highlighted the importance of restoring Syria's energy infrastructure for economic recovery and explored opportunities for future EU engagement in the energy sector with other international partners.

Background

After the fall of the Assad regime at the end of December 2024 and following the Brussels IX Conference of 17 March 2025, Syria and the EU launched the SPCF, which provides a platform to align partners' support on Syria's recovery priorities and coordinate on their implementation.

The Forum is instrumental in facilitating structured engagement among key partners, including EU Member States, the G7, Arab nations, and International Financial Institutions. The SPCF is structured under regular senior-official plenary meetings at capital level, and regular practical level.

It builds on the EU's support for Syria's recovery. During her first visit to Damascus in June 2025, Commissioner Šuica announced €175 million to help Syria rebuild its institutions, advance transitional justice and revive its economy. In January 2026, President Ursula von der Leyen announced around €620 million in EU support for 2026–2027 to support recovery and provide humanitarian aid. In May 2026, the Council restored the full application of the EU–Syria Cooperation Agreement, paving the way for stronger trade ties. On 16 November 2026, EU Foreign Ministers supported moving ahead with the EU-Syria Association Agreement.

In December, a Day of Dialogue will take place for the second time in Damascus, organised by the Syrian authorities, Syrian civil society and the EU. It will provide a platform for inclusive dialogue on Syria's transition and the role of civil society.

A peaceful, stable and inclusive Syria is important for Syrians, to the region and to Europe. The EU is ready to deepen its partnership with Syria as Syrians rebuild their country for all citizens. At today’s Forum in Damascus, we focused on what international partners and businesses can do to support the country’s own priorities, so people can find jobs, businesses can reopen and services can further be restored.

items.title: Humanitarian Coordinator calls for strengthened Ebola readiness in South Sudan
items.blurb:
Country: South Sudan
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Juba, 17 November 2026 – The United Nations Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator in South Sudan, Mr. Ramanathan Balakrishnan, has called for increased preparedness and readiness to respond to a potential Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the country.

The call follows a recent full-scale simulation exercise conducted in October 2026 by the Ministry of Health, the National Public Health Institute (NPHI), the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners to assess the country's capacity to detect, notify, investigate and respond to a potential EVD outbreak.

The exercise assessed key areas of South Sudan’s Ebola preparedness efforts, including case management, infection prevention and control, laboratory capacity, contact tracing and coordination. While the exercise demonstrated the system’s capacity to quickly detect simulated cases, significant gaps remain in alert management, rapid response team management, health worker remuneration, ambulance services, laboratory facilities, personal protective equipment supplies, contact tracing, and screening arrangements at points of entry.

To address these challenges, the Humanitarian Coordinator has launched a three-month prioritised plan to mobilise financial resources to address the operational and capacity gaps identified during the simulation exercise. He called on donors and partners to support the plan, which requests USD$7 million to strengthen preparedness and response capacities.

“While there are no reported cases of Ebola in South Sudan, closing these preparedness gaps is critical to ensure that South Sudan is better prepared to detect, contain and respond to a potential outbreak, and to protect the lives and well-being of its people,” Mr. Balakrishnan said.

Reiterating the importance of national government leadership in strengthening EVD preparedness, Mr. Balakrishnan said, “The payment of health worker salaries by the government authorities is critical, as is facilitating access for Ebola-related movements for both health actors and UNMISS and ensuring the safety and security of humanitarian workers.”

items.title: World: ACNUR presenta un nuevo portal de datos sobre refugiados para reforzar la evidencia e impulsar soluciones para millones de personas desplazadas
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

GINEBRA – En un momento en el que la información fragmentada y la narrativa sesgada sobre el desplazamiento forzado corren el riesgo de influir en decisiones que afectan a millones de personas, ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, presentó hoy su nuevo Portal de Datos sobre refugiados, un punto de acceso único y abierto a datos fiables y verificados sobre personas refugiadas, desplazadas por la fuerza y apátridas.

Por primera vez, el portal recopila estadísticas demográficas junto con información sobre las condiciones de vida, las necesidades de protección y la situación socioeconómica de las personas desplazadas, ofreciendo una visión más completa del desplazamiento, su magnitud, los retos a los que se enfrentan las personas y los avances que se están logrando hacia la búsqueda de soluciones.

Desde datos sobre la pobreza y la matriculación escolar hasta la nutrición, el acceso al agua potable y otros indicadores de bienestar, el portal ofrece una visión más amplia de lo que significa que una persona esté desplazada.

“Detrás de cada dato hay una persona, una experiencia vivida y un futuro. Disponer de datos fiables es esencial para garantizar que las decisiones que tomamos protejan la seguridad de las personas, respeten su dignidad y les brinden oportunidades para prosperar”, afirmó Edem Wosornu, Alta Comisionada Auxiliar para la Protección de ACNUR.

En consonancia con la visión “50 para 35” de ACNUR, cuyo objetivo es reducir a la mitad el número de personas desplazadas por la fuerza que dependen de la asistencia humanitaria para 2035, esta base empírica más amplia ayudará a los gobiernos, a los socios para el desarrollo y a las organizaciones humanitarias a medir los avances hacia la autosuficiencia y las soluciones, evaluar si las políticas y los programas están mejorando la vida de los refugiados, identificar las desigualdades persistentes y las deficiencias operativas, y determinar dónde se necesitan más medidas e inversiones.

Por ejemplo, los datos comparables sobre pobreza disponibles a través del portal para diez países muestran que las tasas de pobreza entre las personas refugiadas superan sistemáticamente a las de las comunidades de acogida, oscilando entre alrededor del 10 por ciento y más del 90 por ciento en los datos recopilados entre 2018 y 2024.

Gracias a una experiencia de usuario moderna e integrada, el Portal de Datos sobre refugiados de ACNUR permitirá a los usuarios explorar, acceder, reutilizar e integrar los datos en sus propios análisis, informes y procesos de toma de decisiones.

Periodistas e investigadores pueden recurrir a información fiable para investigar tendencias, situar las cifras de desplazamiento en su contexto, y elaborar reportajes y análisis basados en pruebas. El nuevo portal permitirá la integración de los datos sobre desplazamiento en sus otras plataformas, mapas, informes y herramientas digitales a través de interfaces de programación de aplicaciones (API) abiertas.

El portal también está diseñado para funcionar con otras plataformas de datos, incluido el Sistema de Datos Comunes de las Naciones Unidas, lo que crea oportunidades para conectar datos sobre personas refugiadas con estadísticas de desarrollo más amplias y comparar las circunstancias de los refugiados con las del conjunto de la población en ámbitos como educación, empleo, salud, financiación y otros aspectos de la vida.

El lanzamiento del portal también supone un paso importante en la transformación digital más amplia de ACNUR. Mediante la consolidación de sistemas de datos fragmentados y la adopción de estándares de datos modernos, la automatización y la inteligencia artificial, la organización pretende que su infraestructura de datos sea más predictiva, eficiente y capaz de responder a las necesidades actuales.

“No se trata solo de una actualización tecnológica, sino de una inversión estratégica en un enfoque más sostenible, adaptable y eficiente de la gestión de datos, que reduce la fragmentación y facilita el mantenimiento, el desarrollo y la mejora de los sistemas a lo largo del tiempo”, afirmó Wosornu. “En última instancia, el Portal de Datos sobre refugiados de ACNUR se basa en una convicción sencilla pero poderosa: la información fiable puede cambiar la forma en que el mundo entiende el desplazamiento y cómo responde ante el”.

Al situar los datos y las pruebas fiables en el centro del debate mundial sobre el desplazamiento forzado, ACNUR pretende reforzar la confianza, respaldar políticas e inversiones más eficaces y contribuir a que una comprensión más profunda del desplazamiento se traduzca en acciones duraderas y significativas.

El Portal de Datos sobre refugiados se ha desarrollado con el apoyo del Centro Conjunto de Datos sobre Desplazamiento Forzado del Banco Mundial y ACNUR.

Nota para editoras y editores:

La versión actual del Portal de Datos sobre refugiados incluye un conjunto limitado de funciones y contenidos. La plataforma seguirá desarrollándose en 2027 y, con el tiempo, se irán añadiendo conjuntos de datos, páginas por país y contenidos temáticos adicionales. Como parte de este proceso, los portales de datos existentes de ACNUR se irán retirando progresivamente en los próximos meses.

items.title: Same City, Different Sources of Pollution: What Ahmedabad’s Air Data Reveals
items.blurb: A patch of dust near a busy road, smoke rising from an industrial chimney, and waste burning in an open space may all contribute to a city's air pollution. But the sources responsible for poor air quality are not necessarily the same across neighbourhoods. This means that a measure addressing pollution in one part of a city may not be equally effective elsewhere. Understanding what contributes to poor air quality at specific locations is therefore an important part of planning cleaner cities . Ahmedabad is attempting to address this challenge by looking beyond citywide air-quality readings and examining pollution at specific locations. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring initiative called SMART-VAYU. Reported by The Times of India (TOI) on September 30, 2026, the project aims to identify local pollution hotspots, trace the sources of emissions and generate data that can help civic authorities plan targeted interventions. Initial monitoring exercises at two locations — Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium — have already revealed how pollution sources can differ within the same city. One city, two different pollution profiles The initial findings from Ahmedabad offer an interesting look at how the sources contributing to air pollution can vary from one location to another. In its October 17, 2026 report, TOI detailed the findings from air-quality sampling at the Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium. Sampling at the riverfront was conducted between May 4 and May 24, while monitoring at Narendra Modi Stadium took place between June 25 and August 8. At the Sabarmati Riverfront, dust accounted for 36% of the estimated source contribution, compared with 23% at Narendra Modi Stadium. Coal combustion contributed 24% at the riverfront, while its estimated contribution at the stadium was just 1%. The pattern was different at Motera. The combined category of marine emissions and refuse burning accounted for 38% of the estimated pollution sources at Narendra Modi Stadium, compared with 16% at the riverfront. Power plant-related sources contributed another 20% at the stadium. The analysis also examined different types of organic aerosols. Traffic-related organic aerosols contributed 18% at Narendra Modi Stadium and 13% at the riverfront. Solid-fuel combustion-related organic aerosols accounted for 16% at the stadium and 5% at the riverfront. These findings highlight an important aspect of urban air pollution: even within one city, different locations can have different pollution profiles . Understanding these differences can help authorities identify which sources need attention in specific areas, rather than approaching air pollution as a uniform problem across the city. Why Ahmedabad is looking beyond citywide AQI readings Identifying the sources behind air pollution is not always straightforward. Citywide air-quality readings provide information about pollution levels, but understanding what is contributing to poor air quality in a particular neighbourhood requires more detailed monitoring. This is the gap that SMART-VAYU aims to address. The initiative stands for Sensing and Monitoring for Air Quality using Real-time Technology – Vision-based Ahmedabad air analysis for Urban Management. The project involves three broad components: mapping existing pollution sources, establishing a hyperlocal monitoring network and developing a decision-support system for urban air-quality management. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. Photograph: (Ahmedabad Mirror) For this, AMC and IIT Kanpur finalised 10 monitoring locations across Ahmedabad. These include Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex, Narendra Modi Stadium, Gujarat Police Academy at Karai, Sanskardham, Veer Savarkar Sports Complex, Pirana AMC community service centre, Rakhial AMC health office, Vatva GIDC's Chandrakala complex, Bopal urban health centre and Thaltej AMC ward office. The selection considered meteorological conditions, particulate matter readings, annual wind patterns, satellite-based aerosol optical depth and estimated PM2.5 concentrations. Practical requirements such as electricity, security, accessibility and airflow were also taken into account. The plan is to deploy five locations with mobile laboratory sampling alongside sensors, while the remaining five will have fixed sensors. The wider project envisages eventually expanding the network to around 400 sensors across Ahmedabad. How the monitoring network will identify pollution sources Unlike conventional monitoring systems that primarily provide broader air-quality readings, these sensors will continuously measure pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide. They will also record meteorological parameters, including temperature and humidity. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring. Photograph: (Hindustan Times) An important component is the mobile Real-Time Source Apportionment Laboratory (RTSA), which will help examine the contribution of different pollution sources. Source apportionment is the process of estimating how much different sources contribute to the pollutants present in the air. These could include vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road dust, construction and waste burning. By examining these contributions, the initiative aims to generate pollution hotspot maps, forecasts and alerts that can help authorities identify locations requiring attention. From identifying pollution to planning targeted action Ahmedabad already has an air-quality monitoring network under the Centre's System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting and Research (SAFAR) programme. Its monitoring stations provide city-level air-quality information and forecasts. SMART-VAYU seeks to add another layer of information by examining pollution sources at specific locations. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. For instance, identifying road dust as a major contributor could inform dust-control and road-cleaning measures. Similarly, evidence of industrial emissions or waste burning could help direct inspections and enforcement. The effectiveness of the initiative will depend on how consistently the monitoring network operates, whether its findings translate into enforceable measures and how improvements in air quality are tracked over time. Ultimately, Ahmedabad's initiative highlights why tackling urban air pollution requires more than understanding how polluted a city is. It also requires knowing what is polluting different parts of it. Because when pollution sources vary from one neighbourhood to another, the solutions must account for those differences too. items.title: TRYING HARD TO LOSE WEIGHT?BUT IS YOUR BODY PUSHING BACK?
items.blurb: “Just eat less.” “Work harder.” “Have some willpower.” We hear it all the time. But if weight loss were that simple, why can keeping it off feel even harder? Because sometimes, your own biology pushes back. After you lose weight, your body can respond with stronger hunger signals and lower energy use. These biological adaptations can favour weight regain. Does that mean weight always comes back? No. It means long-term medical support may need more than a short burst of willpower. And struggling doesn’t mean someone is lazy or lacks discipline. Weight is shaped by biology, behaviour and environment. If you keep struggling, continue with practical nutrition, movement, strength and sleep habits. And if weight repeatedly returns, or the plan feels impossible to sustain, speak to a qualified doctor about long-term weight management and the biological or practical barriers involved. Getting medical support is not failure. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight management. items.blurb: Festive decorations bring colour and warmth to a home, but a little greenery can make the space feel even more inviting. If you want to give your living room, entrance, or balcony a fresh look this festive season, tall indoor plants are a lovely way to do it. They add height, fill empty corners, and bring a natural charm to your decorations. Pair them with earthen pots, warm fairy lights, or a few diyas , and these plants can become part of your festive decor. Here are 10 tall houseplants worth considering. Money Tree The money tree is loved for its distinctive braided trunk and clusters of green leaves. Usually associated with prosperity and good fortune, it makes a fitting addition to festive homes. items.title: Millions Had His Painting. Few Knew His Name!
items.blurb: Copy: For over five decades, his artwork found a place in millions of Indian homes, becoming a familiar sight across generations. Artist S.M. Srinivasan, who passed away at 86, was known for his paintings of deities, especially his two iconic depictions of Lord Venkateswara, which became widely recognised through calendars, posters and framed prints. Born in Kovilpatti, Tamil Nadu, Srinivasan studied up to Class 10 before learning the art of painting under renowned artist Kondaiah Raju. In 1970, he got a rare opportunity to observe and paint the idol at the Tirumala temple. He created two versions, one with elaborate ornaments and another without them. Approved by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD), his paintings were reproduced as calendars, posters and framed prints. Soon, his artwork became a familiar sight on calendars across India, finding its way into homes, shops and everyday spaces. For generations, these familiar images became part of India’s visual and cultural landscape. items.title: ‘I Thought I Was Bad at Art’: How a Museum Is Changing the Way Children See Their Creativity
items.blurb: “I felt that there were opportunities to draw and participate in school activities, but there were fewer chances for children to showcase their work to a wider audience.” For 18-year-old Sahil Santosh Kundojwar, art was something he enjoyed creating but mostly shared with teachers, friends, and family. He had opportunities to draw at school, but finding an audience beyond his immediate circle was not easy. That changed in July 2024, when a teacher at The Aditya Birla Public School in Awarpur, Maharashtra, introduced him to the Children’s Art Museum of India (CAMI). He submitted a drawing of Ganpati Bappa for a theme called ‘My Superhero’. It won a prize, giving him the encouragement to share more of his work. “I didn’t expect to win a prize, so receiving recognition for my Ganpati artwork was a very special and motivating experience for me,” he says. His story reflects the idea behind CAMI, a digital museum that gives children a dedicated space to display their artwork. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, the platform has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. Its collection includes over 20,000 artworks, and the website has received more than a million visitors from over 200 towns and cities. The idea began with a question the siblings found themselves asking during COVID-19. Children were creating art at home, but where could they go to have it seen, appreciated, and preserved? A museum of their own During the pandemic, the siblings were spending more time at home and creating art themselves. They noticed that children around them were doing the same, but much of this work stayed in school notebooks, folders, or at home, with few opportunities to reach a wider audience. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, CAMI has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. They felt that children’s artwork should not be limited to occasional displays at school exhibitions or relegated to a corner of a museum primarily meant for adults. They wanted to build a space where young artists would be at the centre. Krish recalls the question that set the idea in motion. “Why wasn’t there a space where a child could say, ‘This is my artwork, and it belongs in a museum’?” Krish, now 16 and a Class 11 student at The Shri Ram School in Gurugram, and Manya, 19, who is pursuing a bachelor’s degree in the United States, began working on the idea together. For the 16-year-old, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. “I wanted to create a space where children could see their artwork displayed, feel that it mattered, and know that it deserved to be seen,” he says. Manya wanted the experience to feel different from uploading an image online. “We did not want to create just another website where children could upload pictures. We wanted the artwork to have a context and a sense of recognition,” she tells The Better India . Turning that idea into a functioning museum meant learning almost everything from scratch. The siblings began with an Excel spreadsheet, mapping out how children would submit their work and how the museum would organise and display it. They experimented with WordPress and Wix to build early versions of the website and emailed schools and children to gauge interest. There was no established organisation or technical team behind them. They learnt about website development, communication, curation, and outreach as they went along, with their parents helping them through the early stages. “The first step was deciding that we were going to build it rather than keep talking about it,” Krish says. The website went live in January 2022. Its first version was uncomplicated, allowing children to submit artwork and have it displayed in an online collection. The first submission was a picture of a peacock sent in by a young child. Because the website did not yet require all the details it collects today, the founders knew very little about the artist. They have even tried to trace her since. Krish remembers the submission for what it represented. “There was just a child who had created something and wanted a place to share it,” he says. Where young artists find recognition As children began finding the platform, CAMI grew beyond its original digital collection. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. One such initiative is the monthly ArtFest. Each edition revolves around a theme or creative prompt, which children can interpret in their own way before submitting their artwork. Selected entries are showcased as part of the programme. For Krish, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. The idea is to encourage participation rather than make creativity depend on winning a competition. Manya says the team wanted children to have opportunities to return to the platform and keep experimenting. “We realised that children should not have to wait for one opportunity to submit their artwork. We wanted our initiative to give them regular reasons to create, participate, and explore,” she says. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries , ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. These programmes allow students to display their work beyond the classroom. Its collaborations include Sarvodaya schools in Delhi, the Aditya Birla Group, and Bagiya Foundation. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. Each entry goes through a verification process to ensure it is appropriate for children. Art teachers, curators, and members of the core team review submissions, generally within 24 to 48 hours. The team considers originality, effort, and creative expression rather than expecting professional-level technique. Accepted artwork becomes part of the digital collection or may be considered for an ArtFest, exhibition, or school gallery. Children also receive a CAMI certificate. “We are not looking for technical perfection. A child’s artwork does not need to look professionally executed to have value,” explains the teen founder. The museum has also developed a learning section with resources on creating, appreciating, and understanding different art forms. These include traditional and indigenous Indian styles such as Warli, Madhubani, and Pattachitra. Children and visitors can also engage with CAMI through its YouTube channel and Spotify podcast. In 2023, the founders took the museum into another digital environment by launching a virtual museum on Roblox. With more than 120 million daily active users globally, the platform offered a way to reach children in a space where they already play, create, and connect. The virtual museum allows players to walk through galleries and view artwork made by children. It has received over 2,70,600 visits, extending the reach of the collection beyond the conventional website. What recognition can mean to a young artist? For the founders, the value of the initiative is not measured only through membership figures or the number of artworks in its collection. Some of the most meaningful moments have come through the responses they receive from children. Manya remembers an Instagram message from a girl who was around 12. After seeing her painting displayed in the museum, the child wrote, “I used to think I wasn’t good at art, but when you displayed my painting in the museum, I began to feel that maybe I was,” she recalls. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. The message stayed with the co-founder because it showed how being taken seriously could change a child’s perception of their own ability. “She was not suddenly a professional artist, and nothing about her artistic ability had changed overnight. What changed was that someone had taken her work seriously enough to give it a place,” she says. Manya has also seen how children’s creative expression changes as they continue making and sharing art. Some begin with familiar drawings of two mountains and the sun, but gradually experiment with portraits, posters, different compositions, and styles such as cubism and modern art. “For me, that progression is not really about becoming a ‘better’ artist in a technical sense. It is about becoming more confident in having an idea of their own and being willing to experiment with it,” she says. Seventeen-year-old Kritika from Delhi has experienced some of that encouragement herself. Before joining CAMI in September this year, she mostly shared her artwork with family or during school art classes. She wanted to see her work displayed alongside that of other children and hoped for feedback that would help her take herself seriously as an artist. Her first submission, titled ‘Fish Illusion’, was accepted for the online gallery. Seeing it published encouraged her to begin working on another project. “When I first submitted my artwork on the website, I hoped that my work would be accepted and displayed on a real platform. I wanted to see how it looked alongside other children’s art and hoped to get some encouragement or feedback that would make me feel like a real artist,” she says. Her parents’ response to the painting also stayed with her. They complimented her use of colours and told her that the artwork had brought a smile to their faces. “That made me realise that my art has the power to make people happy,” she adds. Having her work displayed on the platform has made her more comfortable sharing it with others. “Now, I feel incredibly proud to show people my work and confidently call myself an artist,” she says. Sahil, too, explains that the recognition he received through CAMI made him more confident about putting his work forward. Appreciation from teachers and classmates after winning the Monthly Best Prize encouraged him to participate in more activities. He has one piece of advice for young artists. “I would tell them not to be afraid or shy about showing their work. If you are proud of what you have created, you should share it with others because your creativity is special and unique . Don’t worry about whether everyone will like it,” he says. Building a community across India As the initiative developed its programmes, its reach began extending beyond the founders’ immediate circles. What started with children from familiar schools and communities now includes participants from major cities as well as smaller towns and villages. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries, ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. The founders cite participation from places such as Vaniyambadi, Rampurhat, Guntur, Nainital, Khammam, Ranaghat, Patna, Bareilly, Nagpur, Coimbatore, Kanhagad, Prayagraj, Kota, and Puducherry. The platform has also reached villages in Uttarakhand and smaller communities in West Bengal and Odisha. Manya says the geographical spread has been one of the most surprising aspects of the journey. A digital museum, she explains, allows a child from a smaller town to participate in the same collection as someone living in a major city. The first major sign that CAMI was gaining momentum came by June 2022, when the team began receiving artwork submissions every day. Its first school collaboration showed the founders that they could reach groups of children through educators, rather than relying only on individual submissions. The Roblox museum, launched the following year, opened another route to young audiences. The initiative now has a core team of five members, supported by more than 20 volunteers and over 500 young brand ambassadors. It continues to operate as a bootstrapped initiative, with the founders relying on their own resources and family support rather than institutional venture funding. Their roles have changed as the museum has grown. Krish, who initially handled everything from the website and social media to school outreach and submissions, now focuses more on its development, operations, and future direction. Manya’s responsibilities centre on ideation, marketing, outreach, and programme development. Building the initiative while studying has also taught them to manage their time and share responsibilities. Krish works on the initiative after school and during weekends, while prioritising academics during examinations. As the team has expanded, he has learnt to delegate rather than remain involved in every task. “I often say that school taught me how to learn, but CAMI taught me how to turn ideas into something real,” he says. The siblings are now looking at ways to create more opportunities for young artists. These include exhibitions, local art initiatives led by ambassadors and avenues through which children can have their artwork commissioned. The co-founder sees this as a natural next step for a platform built around recognising young people’s creativity. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. “If we tell children that their creative work has value, we should also think about how we can create real opportunities around that value,” he says. From an Excel spreadsheet and a simple website to a community of more than 3 lakh registered members, CAMI has grown considerably since 2022. At its core, it continues to champion the idea that children’s creativity deserves to be taken seriously , giving young artists the encouragement and recognition to keep creating. Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone
items.blurb:
He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare

  • Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report?

It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone.

What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security.

items.title: Menopause symptoms aren’t always taken seriously. These female lawmakers plan to change that
items.blurb:
From Utah to Louisiana, US states are making menopause care more affordable and accessible for midlife women

Melissa Shusterman was desperate for help with her menopausal symptoms: body aches, lethargy and brain fog, which she described as feeling “not myself”. The Pennsylvania state representative saw a gynecologist, a physical therapist, a chiropractor and a urologist. One doctor gave her lubricant, even though she’d already explained to him that sex was not the problem. (“Have you seen my husband?” she quipped.)

“I am more than lubrication,” Shusterman said. “I am a dynamic, smart, hardworking woman who wants to continue to feel good, so I can join my contemporaries, get back to work, and change things.”
